Dataset scope: 12,343 records, 6 countries, 10 job titles, 9 primary skills, years 2015–2035.

Most critical takeaways (data-derived)

  • Automation pressure rises across the horizon
    Average AI risk increases from 0.295 in 2015 to 0.508 in 2035.
  • Pay grows, but not uniformly across risk
    Overall median salary rises from $24,247 to $36,763, while salary and AI risk are negatively correlated (overall r=-0.245).
  • Job survival weakens in aggregate
    The share of records with job_survival_class≥1 declines from 91.1% to 83.7%.
  • Demand shifts toward a small set of durable skills
    From 2015 to 2035, the fastest growth in average skill demand is led by Java (+3.95).
  • Openings expand modestly overall
    Total job openings rise from 14,024,622 to 14,838,117 across the dataset.

Limitations: This dataset is synthetic (trend-based simulation). Results should be interpreted as scenario-style signals rather than observed labor-market measurements. Salary values are in USD and do not adjust for purchasing power.

Salary Trends & Segmentation

Salary × automation risk relationship

Across the full dataset, salary and AI risk are negatively correlated (Pearson r=-0.245). In the latest year (2035), the correlation is r=-0.411. This indicates higher-risk work in this dataset tends to sit in lower-pay bands, though the relationship varies by year.

Note: scatter uses a sample for readability; correlation values use the full dataset.

Skills Demand & Future-Proofing

Growth is computed as average skill_demand_score in 2035 minus 2015 for each primary_skill present in both endpoint years.

Job Survival & Market Outlook

How to read this section

Job survival rate is computed as the share of records with job_survival_class ≥ 1 within each segment. The class mix chart shows how the composition shifts over time.

Use these views to identify segments where risk rises faster than compensation and openings, which can signal exposure to automation substitution.

Strategic Recommendations

Recommendations are tied to the measured shifts in risk, salary, skills, survival, and openings shown above.

  • Prioritize risk-weighted workforce planning
    Use the rising average AI risk (0.295→0.508) to re-balance roles toward lower-risk, higher-survival categories and redesign high-risk workflows rather than backfilling like-for-like.
  • Align compensation strategy with risk exposure
    Given the negative salary–risk relationship (overall r=-0.245; 2035 r=-0.411), treat high-risk roles as candidates for automation augmentation, and reserve premium pay for roles combining lower risk with strong survival rates.
  • Target reskilling into skills with sustained demand growth
    Allocate reskilling budgets toward the highest-growth skills from 2015 to 2035 (e.g., top movers in the growth chart), and de-emphasize skills with declining demand in this dataset.
  • Segment interventions by experience level
    Entry-level survival rates trail senior levels throughout the horizon; concentrate early-career pathways on higher- survival skill clusters and structured apprenticeship-style upskilling.
  • Build geography-aware talent strategies
    Salary and risk trajectories vary by country; use the country trend view (top countries by openings) to localize hiring plans and training investments.
